edits.find: Estrogen raises thyroxine-binding globulin, and β-hCG (which shares an alpha subunit with TSH) stimulates the TSH receptor — so a normal pregnancy makes more thyroxine on its own. Waiting for the TSH to rise is the tested wrong move.

edits.find: Two stem facts close the question. TSH 110 with T4 0.6 puts the lesion below the pituitary — the feedback loop is intact and screaming, so panhypopituitarism is excluded outright and neonatal Graves (which runs TSH-suppressed with high T4) is excluded in the opposite direction. Among the primary causes, the exam is silent on goiter and the maternal history is clean (balanced diet, prenatal vitamins), which strips the two goitrous mechanisms — dyshormonogenesis and iodine deficiency — of their tell and leaves the default: dysgenesis (agenesis, hypoplasia, or an ectopic gland arrested along the thyroglossal tract). The home birth is not a cause; it explains only why a screen-detected, asymptomatic diagnosis instead presented at one month, as maternal T4 washed out.

edits.find: High TSH, low T4, no goiter is dysgenesis; a goiter means a synthesis defect, and a low TSH means the pituitary. · Symptom onset at weeks-to-months, not at birth, is the fingerprint of congenital hypothyroidism — placental maternal T4 covers the first weeks, so a normal newborn exam never reassures. · Unconjugated jaundice past 2 weeks of age earns a thyroid and a galactosemia thought; conjugated jaundice at any age earns a biliary one. · Macroglossia plus hoarse cry equals mucopolysaccharide deposition — the exam's shorthand for hypothyroid soft tissue, distinct from Beckwith-Wiedemann (macroglossia with hemihyperplasia and hypoglycemia ⚠︎). · Treat on the screening result; imaging to name the cause never delays levothyroxine, because the neurodevelopmental window is measured in weeks (in-context: no deficits when treatment begins in the neonatal period). · A goiter in a hypothyroid newborn reroutes you to a synthesis problem or an iodine problem — dysgenesis has no gland to enlarge. · In central hypothyroidism, give cortisol before levothyroxine: thyroid hormone accelerates cortisol clearance and can precipitate adrenal crisis ⚠︎.

edits.find:
The stem names the lesion for you: retinal hemangioblastoma, bilateral. That single identification closes the question, because no other option on the list produces one — NF1 gives optic gliomas and Lisch nodules, MEN2B gives conjunctival and corneal neuromas, Sturge-Weber gives a leptomeningeal and choroidal vascular malformation, and Li-Fraumeni gives sarcomas with no characteristic eye finding. The mother's resected adrenal tumor is the second half of the answer rather than a decoy: it reads as a pheochromocytoma transmitted in autosomal dominant fashion, and hemangioblastoma plus adrenal medullary tumor is the von Hippel-Lindau organ pattern, with clear cell renal carcinoma the third member. The facial patch is what the question is actually testing — a single light brown macule is a normal café-au-lait spot, not the multiple macules of NF1 and not a red-purple port-wine stain.

The same move works on a different lesion. A teenager found confused after an unwitnessed fall, with a fibroma growing from under a toenail and calcified nodules lining the lateral ventricles on CT, has tuberous sclerosis complex: the fall was a seizure, the nodules are subependymal hamartomas, and the nail lesion is a periungual fibroma, which appears in adolescence. NF1 puts neurofibromas on the trunk and a glioma on the optic nerve, ataxia-telangiectasia starts with ataxia in early childhood, and the nail-bed sign of endocarditis is a splinter hemorrhage, not a fibroma.
